newsitem.title: USA: New sex charges filed against U.S. Army trainer.
newsitem.headline: New sex charges filed against U.S. Army trainer.

text.p: The U.S. Army said on Friday it had filed nine new charges, including 16 counts of rape, against a drill instructor accused in a sexual misconduct scandal at the Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.

The new charges against Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, an instructor at a training facility at the proving ground, range from rape to inappropriate comments and cover a period of two years, the Army said.
Of the 16 rape counts contained in the new charges, eight refer to one female soldier, three to another, and the remaining five refer to five different soldiers, the Army said.
Including earlier charges, Simpson is accused of a total of 25 counts of rape.
He is also accused in the newest filings with forcible sodomy, theft, extortion, battery, indecent assault, maltreatment and other violations.
The charges say Simpson stole a watch from one female soldier and a gold necklace from another.
Simpson had deferred entering a plea, in line with military court tradition, at an arraignment on the earlier charges on Dec. 6. His court martial trial has been scheduled to begin in February.
Attorneys for Simpson and others accused in the scandal have accused the Army of making public comments and taking actions that make it difficult for their clients to receive a fair trial.
Simpson is the only of three trainers charged with military olaw violations in the scandal at Aberdeen to have been jailed since the first charges were filed.
A total of 20 soldiers at the Aberdeen base have been implicated in the misconduct scandal, and authorities said that number could rise to as many as 25 as the investigation continues.
The scandal has also set off an Army-wide examination of sexual harassment.
Two drill sergeants at Fort Leonard Wood, Mo., were punished for lesser assaults on recruits and a third was cleared of charges of sexual misconduct.
On Wednesday, the Army's top commander said that drill sergeants guilty of rape were exceptional "bad apples" but less serious sex harassment was a widespread problem the Army knew how to fix.
Army Chief of Staff Gen. Dennis Reimer said there may be systemic problems at Army training centres, such as too few officers and chaplains for recruits to hear sex misconduct complaints.
He also said higher officers at Aberdeen failed to deal with the drill sergeants' alleged sexual abuse of recruits.
